Key finding: The permissions.html "Permission Model constraints" says "The model does not inherit to a worker thread." But SECURITY.md says "Workers inherit the permission restrictions of their parent process. Passing an empty or modified execArgv to a worker does not grant it additional permissions." That's a conflict. Also permissions.html states --env-file is not subject to permission model rules (documented fact). Also existing file descriptors via node:fs bypass the Permission Model. Also symlinks followed; relative symlinks may allow access to arbitrary files — and "you must ensure that no paths to which access has been granted contain relative symbolic links." Wildcard semantics: /srv/jobs/*.js — "After passing a wildcard character (*) all subsequent characters will be ignored. For example: /home/*.js will work similar to /home/*." So --allow-fs-read=/srv/jobs/*.js grants read to everything under /srv/jobs (approximately), not just .js files. Big correction.

Also the entrypoint included: the job script path is the entrypoint presumably, so it's included in the allow list automatically. Actually the launcher loads jobs — the job js file is an entrypoint? The launcher is the entrypoint; the job .js is loaded via require/import, which needs FS read permission — hence --allow-fs-read. Fine.

Also, "This feature does not protect against malicious code" and "does not provide security guarantees in the presence of malicious code. Malicious code can bypass the permission model and execute arbitrary code." So the answer: cannot certify; not a tenant isolation boundary.

Also --allow-worker is dangerous: workers are not permission-inherited (per constraints page), so enabling workers with untrusted code... Actually the conflict.
